info.bio:
The Stone Roses es una banda originaria de Mánchester, Reino Unido, la más representativa del movimiento Madchester de finales de los '80. Es uno de los grupos que más influyó a bandas de la escena Britpop en los '90.

Su música se caracteriza por tener atractivas melodías 'beatlescas' combinadas al sonido dance beat de la época. Con apenas un par de singles obtuvieron una aureola de culto y la prensa especializada los trató con reverencia.

scenes.name: Madchester y ambient house
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Un movimiento de Manchester que marca la música de baile como ningún otro de los ochenta: la fusión de psicodelia, techno y pop. KLF importa el acid house; los Stone Roses mezclan ritmos disco hipnóticos, melodías pegadizas y entusiasmo sesentero; los Happy Mondays de Shaun Ryder (Bummed) y Black Grape; Charlatans, Nitzer Ebb, Shamen, Pop Will Eat Itself, Jesus Jones. Más allá de la moda, 808 State (herederos de Kraftwerk, «Pacific State»), William Orbit, Richard Kirk, A Guy Called Gerald, el collage de Coldcut y Primal Scream (Screamadelica).
scenes.family: Soul, funk, disco, hip hop y baile

scenes.name: Mánchester: la Haçienda y Madchester
scenes.book: Techno Rebels: The Renegades of Electronic Funk
scenes.author: Dan Sicko
scenes.desc: En 1988, fuera del círculo de Rhythm King, había que ir a Mánchester para oír discos de Detroit: en la Haçienda (financiada por New Order) Mike Pickering, criado en el soul, pinchaba «Goodbye Kiss», «Groovin’ without a Doubt» o «Triangle of Love» antes que nadie en Londres, donde en el Spectrum no sonaban. La ciudad de los Smiths, The Fall y New Order unió el indie al acid house con los Happy Mondays, los Stone Roses e Inspiral Carpets, un puente hacia 808 State y A Guy Called Gerald.

podcast.title: John Peel Sessions (Spring 1988)
podcast.body: John Peel, a pivotal figure in modern music, featured The Stone Roses in Peel Sessions during the spring of 1988. These sessions were instrumental in disseminating the Manchester movement throughout the United Kingdom. "cuando John Pill saca pilsesiones de los Happy Mondays de los Stone Roses y de todas estas bandas ya pues incluso tenemos sesiones en música, Jaws, Guy Collierad, en la spillsession que era algo muy raro de ver, ya eso se es parce por todo el Reino Unido."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Attack on FM Revolver Offices (1990)
podcast.body: On January 30, 1990, The Stone Roses launched a "grudge attack" on the offices of their former indie label, FM Revolver, and its president Paul Birch and his girlfriend Olivia, storming the premises with cans of blue and white paint. The incident, which caused $50,000 in damage to the offices and saw Birch's Mercedes vandalized with "free bodywork" and a brick through the windshield, led to the band's arrest the following day and subsequent vandalism charges; in March 1990, a judge fined each member $3,000 but spared them jail, fearing notoriety. "On January 30th, 1990, they launched a grudge attack on the offices of FM revolver president Paul Birch and his girlfriend, you know, just kind of teach him a lesson."

srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 2

podcast.title: Spike Island Concert (May 27, 1990)
podcast.body: This outdoor concert at Spike Island, a peninsula in the Mersey River surrounded by chemical factories and power plants on a reclaimed chemical dump, was proclaimed "the gig of the year" upon its announcement. Despite being considered an "average or even below average" performance by the band, who seemed nervous and tentative, it drew their largest crowd (28,000-30,000 people). The event became legendary because it was a pivotal "meeting of the minds" for "Madchester kids" and "rave kids," fostered by ecstasy, and was heavily hyped by the British music press as the start of the 90s. "The line they took was, the 90s begin now. Ain't it great?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Spike Island Concert (May 27, 1990)
podcast.body: On May 27, 1990, The Stone Roses, hailed as one of the most important British rock bands, played their biggest gig at Spike Island, near Liverpool, on the Mersey River. The event attracted 30,000 "ecstasy field fans" to what was colloquially known as a toxic dump due to a nearby chemical factory causing chemical burns (mistaken for sunburn) and greasy residue in fans' hair. The Stone Roses headlined, coming on at 8 PM to a hero's welcome, marking a significant milestone as 30,000 people attended a concert by an indie band, an unprecedented achievement at the time. "Spike Island, the height of Madchester, the height of ecstasy mania, and the greatest moments in the career of one of the most important British rock bands of all time, the Stone Roses, playing Spike Islands, May 27, 1990."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 8

podcast.title: Spike Island Festival (1990)
podcast.body: On May 27, 1990, The Stone Roses headlined an outdoor festival at Spike Island, a strip of heavily polluted land, drawing an unprecedented 30,000 people who paid about 14 quid each to enter. This massive turnout contrasted sharply with their struggles just twelve months prior to attract 30 people to a bar gig, highlighting their rapid ascent as an indie band. "A year later, May 27, 1990, the Roses had lined an outdoor festival on a strip of once heavily polluted land called Spike Island. Twelve months earlier, they were struggling to get 30 people to show up to a bar gig. This time, though, 30,000 people turned up, paying about 14 quid to get in."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: British Airways Air Rage Conviction (February 13, 1998) – Sentenced to Four Months in Strangeways
podcast.body: Ian Brown boarded British Airways Flight 1611 from Paris to Manchester on February 13, 1998. During the short flight, a dispute arose with flight attendant Christine Cooper when she made what Brown interpreted as a dismissive wave. Brown allegedly shouted at her and threatened to chop off her hands; when the pilot came out to investigate, Brown reportedly repeated the threat. He was also said to have banged on the cockpit door for 20 to 30 seconds during descent. When the plane landed, he was arrested and charged with air rage. At trial in October 1998, Brown's defense — that his remarks were jokes and he never banged on the door — was not believed. On October 23, 1998, he was sentenced to four months at Strangeways prison. Brown maintained he was made an example because of a timing coincidence with a genuine air rage case in Spain, and claimed racism as a factor. "Ian and his friends and supporters maintained that he was set up as an example."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Reunion for Six Years (2011-2017)
podcast.body: The Stone Roses reunited in 2011 and managed to maintain their reunion for six years, joining a significant wave of bands from various eras who got back together in the 21st century. This reunion trend was often driven by the financial opportunities presented by live touring amidst declining CD sales. "and even the stone roses managed to hold it together for six years starting in 2011."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 1: (100-91)

podcast.title: Mani Death (2025) – Distinctive Bass Lines Sung by Audiences Before Vocals Entered
podcast.body: Mani (Gary Mounfield), bassist of Stone Roses and Primal Scream, died in 2025. His bass lines on songs such as "I Wanna Be Adored" were so distinctive and immediately recognizable that audiences would sing them aloud before the vocals even entered. He was a key contributor to the "Madchester" sound. "His bass line in songs like 'I Wanna Be Adored' was so distinctive that the audience sang it before the voice entered."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Awesome Unit Together
podcast.body: The Stone Roses were considered an "awesome unit" when they were together, implying a synergy that was lost upon their split. "The Stone Roses, an awesome unit when they were together."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Biggest UK Indie Band (Early 1990s)
podcast.body: At the beginning of the 1990s, The Stone Roses were recognized as the biggest indie band in the UK. This status was largely driven by the success of their self-titled debut album and their association with the burgeoning Madchester scene. "At the beginning of the 1990s the biggest Indie band in the UK was the Stone Roses."

podcast.title: Claims of Being Set Up
podcast.body: To this day, Ian Brown, along with his friends and supporters, maintains that he was unfairly targeted and set up as an example, asserting that he did not deserve to be sent to jail for the air rage incident. "To this day though, Ian and his friends and supporters maintained that he was set up as some kind of example and did not deserve to be sent to jail."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Local Popularity and Delayed Recordings
podcast.body: Before achieving widespread recognition, The Stone Roses, along with bands like James and Happy Mondays, were giving numerous local concerts in Manchester and had released small singles within the city between 1982 and 1984. Despite being "authentic idols" in Manchester, they took years to record substantial material due to their "completely carefree" nature, a trait that proved incompatible with the demands of major labels later on. "pensé que el mejor osestón Rose o James o los capi-mondes no eran famosos pero sí que ya estaban dando muchos conciertos locales en Manchester ya tenían pequeñas cosas sacadas en síngles dentro de la ciudad de Manchester"

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Early Recognition
podcast.body: The speaker recalled reading about The Stone Roses and immediately recognizing their potential to become a significant band. The radio station's staff enthusiastically supported their music, believing they were leading the culture in Toronto, Ontario, Western New York, and possibly beyond, particularly for British music. "I remember reading about the Happy Mondays and thinking, okay, this band is going to be something along with the stone roses and the charlatans."

srcs.episode: OGHONM 1000th Episode: The Q&A From the Live Recording

podcast.title: Essence Compromised by Major Labels
podcast.body: The band's "carefree" approach, which led them to spend years performing locally as idols without quickly producing recorded material, was incompatible with the commercial pressures of major multinational labels. These labels, in their rush to capitalize on the Manchester sound, ultimately "destroyed" the movement's authentic essence. "no olvidemos que grupos como los Estón Rosos o como los JAPY mondesis tuvieron años en Manchester dando con ciertos y siendo muy populares y indoténticos ídolos en la ciudad sin grabar material porque ellos eran gente completamente dejada entonces no era muy compatible todo esto con las grandes multinacionales y al final puesto a estas multinacionales se lo acabaron cargando."

podcast.title: Holy Trinity of Madchester
podcast.body: The Stone Roses were one of the three bands forming the "Holy Trinity" of the Madchester scene, alongside Happy Mondays and Inspiral Carpets, representing the core of the movement in Manchester in the late 1980s and early 1990s. "Along with the carpets and the stone roses, the Mondays exemplified what madchester was all about."

podcast.title: Ian Brown's Air Rage Conviction
podcast.body: On February 13, 1998, Ian Brown, the then-ex-lead singer of The Stone Roses, was arrested for "air rage" aboard British Airways Flight 1611 from Paris to Manchester. A flight attendant, Christine Cooper, alleged that after a misunderstanding, Brown yelled threats, including that he'd "chop her hands off," and later banged on the cockpit door for 20-30 seconds during the plane's descent. Brown denied the allegations in court, claiming his remarks were jokes and he didn't bang on the door, but was sentenced to four months in the notorious Strangeways Prison. "Ian was sentenced to four months in prison at the notorious Strangeways Prison."

podcast.title: Influential British Band
podcast.body: Emerging from Britain in the late 1980s, The Stone Roses became one of the most popular and influential bands of their time. By 1988, they had developed a new sound that blended 60s pop, 60s psychedelia, and modern dance, perfectly fitting the era of rave and house music in the UK, especially with the popularity of ecstasy. "Out of all the bands to come out of Britain in the late 1980s, no one was more popular and influential than the Stone Roses."

podcast.title: Prison Experience at Strangeways
podcast.body: While serving his four-month sentence at Strangeways Prison, a facility housing 1100 hardcore prisoners, Ian Brown adapted to the conditions. He joked about "turning Muslim" to avoid the "horrible meat pies" and get halal food like lentils, rice, and chicken. Despite guards allegedly trying to turn other prisoners against him, he was popular, giving autographs in exchange for cigarettes and newspapers. Authorities had to frequently move him due to his popularity. He read extensively and maintained physical fitness, doing 500 sit-ups and 400 push-ups daily, emerging in better shape than ever before. "He joked that he, quote, turned Muslim to avoid eating the horrible meat pies they served."

concerts.title: Spike Island (May 27th, 1990) – Legendary Outdoor Gig
concerts.body: This legendary outdoor concert, held on a reclaimed chemical dump on a peninsula by the River Mersey, attracted 28,000 to 30,000 people—the band's largest crowd ever. Despite immense hype and a 15-song set, the performance was generally considered average or below average, marked by nervousness, tentativeness, and a suspect sound system, except for the last ten minutes. Its legendary status is attributed more to the cultural "meeting of the minds" between Madchester and rave kids, and the heavy media hype, rather than the musical quality. "The Stone Roses with something from their 15 song set played at Spike Island on May 27th 1990."

xref.title: Attack on FM Revolver Offices (1990)
xref.body: On January 30, 1990, The Stone Roses launched a "grudge attack" on the offices of their former indie label, FM Revolver, and its president Paul Birch and his girlfriend Olivia, storming the premises with cans of blue and white paint. The incident, which caused $50,000 in damage to the offices and saw Birch's Mercedes vandalized with "free bodywork" and a brick through the windshield, led to the band's arrest the following day and subsequent vandalism charges; in March 1990, a judge fined each member $3,000 but spared them jail, fearing notoriety. "On January 30th, 1990, they launched a grudge attack on the offices of FM revolver president Paul Birch and his girlfriend, you know, just kind of teach him a lesson."

xref.title: Spike Island Festival (1990)
xref.body: On May 27, 1990, The Stone Roses headlined an outdoor festival at Spike Island, a strip of heavily polluted land, drawing an unprecedented 30,000 people who paid about 14 quid each to enter. This massive turnout contrasted sharply with their struggles just twelve months prior to attract 30 people to a bar gig, highlighting their rapid ascent as an indie band. "A year later, May 27, 1990, the Roses had lined an outdoor festival on a strip of once heavily polluted land called Spike Island. Twelve months earlier, they were struggling to get 30 people to show up to a bar gig. This time, though, 30,000 people turned up, paying about 14 quid to get in."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Spike Island Performance (May 27, 1990)
xref.body: On May 27, 1990, The Stone Roses, hailed as one of the most important British rock bands, played their biggest gig at Spike Island, near Liverpool, on the Mersey River. The event attracted 30,000 "ecstasy field fans" to what was colloquially known as a toxic dump due to a nearby chemical factory causing chemical burns (mistaken for sunburn) and greasy residue in fans' hair. The Stone Roses headlined, coming on at 8 PM to a hero's welcome, marking a significant milestone as 30,000 people attended a concert by an indie band, an unprecedented achievement at the time. "Spike Island, the height of Madchester, the height of ecstasy mania, and the greatest moments in the career of one of the most important British rock bands of all time, the Stone Roses, playing Spike Islands, May 27, 1990."

xref.title: British Airways Flight Incident (1998)
xref.body: On February 13, 1998, not long after releasing his first solo album and while estranged from The Stone Roses, Ian Brown boarded British Airways Flight 1611 from Charles de Gaulle Airport to Manchester after an MTV event in Paris. Once airborne, he allegedly got into a row with a flight attendant, threatening to "cut your hands off," and then caused a disturbance by banging on the cockpit door and swearing at the crew during the plane's descent. Upon landing, he was arrested and charged with endangering the safety of an aircraft in flight. "Officially, Ian got into a row with a flight attendant over something, allegedly saying, I'm going to cut your hands off."

xref.title: Andy Rourke Death (May 18, 2023) – Pancreatic Cancer, Age 59; Sued Morrissey, Later Played Two Morrissey Singles
xref.body: Andy Rourke was a founding member of the Smiths and is considered by fans one of the greatest bassists in the history of British indie rock. His time with the band ended badly: a heroin addiction, a lawsuit against Morrissey and Johnny Marr for unpaid royalties (he was broke), and a decade later a bankruptcy over tax issues. Post-Smiths, he worked with the Pretenders, Killing Joke, Stone Roses singer Ian Brown, Dolores O'Riordan and the Cranberries, and Peter Hook of New Order. In a remarkable reconciliation, he played on two Morrissey solo singles despite the money disputes. His father and sister were both diagnosed with cancer, which prompted him to start a cancer charity; he himself was later diagnosed with pancreatic cancer. He died in a New York hospital on May 18, 2023, age 59. "Ask any Smiths fan, and they'll tell you that he was one of the greatest bassists in the history of British Indie Rock."

xref.title: Ian Brown's Air Rage Conviction
xref.body: On February 13, 1998, Ian Brown, the then-ex-lead singer of The Stone Roses, was arrested for "air rage" aboard British Airways Flight 1611 from Paris to Manchester. A flight attendant, Christine Cooper, alleged that after a misunderstanding, Brown yelled threats, including that he'd "chop her hands off," and later banged on the cockpit door for 20-30 seconds during the plane's descent. Brown denied the allegations in court, claiming his remarks were jokes and he didn't bang on the door, but was sentenced to four months in the notorious Strangeways Prison. "Ian was sentenced to four months in prison at the notorious Strangeways Prison."

xref.title: Silvertone Records Dispute
xref.body: Around the time Madchester was ending (early 1990s), The Stone Roses were embroiled in issues with Silvertone Records, which significantly hindered their ability to release new music. "the roses had gotten to their whole silver tone thing and they were unable to get anything together."

xref.title: Spotty Solo Career
xref.body: As the singer of The Stone Roses, Ian Brown's solo career has been described as "extremely spotty," and certainly nothing close to the level of success or impact achieved by The Stone Roses in the early 1990s. "Both have had extremely spotty solo careers, and certainly nothing approaching what the roses were in the early 1990s."
